body:
It's easy to see how Durant would take offense to Ishbia's comments, but there was a bit more context to what the Suns owner was saying
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 18, 2026
                            
                    at
    10:26 am ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Kevin Durant is playing the "blame KD" hashtag card on social media after Suns owner Mat Ishbia went on CNBC and said, "bringing in super talented players like Kevin Durant doesn't necessarily lead to championships." There was a bit more context to Ishbia's comments, which we'll get to, but Durant took offense to the headline and, predictably, fired back at Ishbia. And so ensued the following exchange: Durant: #blameKD even though KD stayed on top of his game at 36 and got u back this "culture" you love so much. Aye, Matthew acts like I got arrested for a DUI or sumn. Back to threads 😂😂😂😂😂😂😂Ishbia: You obviously didn't watch the clip. 😂 Didn't blame you @Kdtrey5, but am happy with the culture we are building here in Phoenix. We got the right guys and right focus now and are excited for this season. ... Good luck this season in Houston.Durant: U should be giving Thanks every chance u get. You don't have to pay me an absurd amount of money to play for another team.So let's address this one comment at a time, beginning with Ishbia's original answer, in its entirety, when he was asked on CNBC what, with the benefit of hindsight, he had learned from the trade his Suns made for Durant two days after his purchase of the team became official in February of 2023. Ishbia's full comments"The team was I think the [No.] 8 or 9 seed [in the Western Conference] when I bought the team," Ishbia said. "We had some good young players, and [the question was]: Can we get over the top? I basically was told, 'Hey, as an owner, stay out of it. Give them some money. And so I said, 'Hey listen, we'll go into the luxury tax, go do whatever it takes to try to win a championship."And so, we did that," Ishbia continued. "But it was more going and getting Kevin Durant. Which ... good player, done a lot of great things, won two championships before, but it was not aligned with my vision. We had a couple years and it did not succeed, as we're well aware of at this point."After that year, I decided [to] trade Kevin Durant, bring in my [own] GM (Brian Gregory replaced James Jones), bring in a new coach (Jordan Ott replaced Mike Budenholzer, who had replaced Frank Vogel), and get extremely involved personally with the type of guy and type of person we want in the organization, not just on the court but off the court."I'm not saying [that type of person is] Kevin Durant or not Kevin Durant, but here's what I will say: It is Dillon Brooks. It is Jordan Goodwin. It is Collin Gillespie. Of course Devin Booker. I'm not going to name every one of my players, but we've defined what matters to us. We have a thing called Suns DNA. The type of player that we believe in, that we want, and it's a team that the fans will be proud of. "Everyone thought we were going to be the worst team in the league last year. We made the playoffs. Won 45 games. We're going to build on that. So what I've learned, my biggest lesson ... it's not positive or negative about Kevin Durant. We have to define what we're about in Phoenix, and then stick with it. And believe in our vision and our path. And I didn't do that in the beginning. I kind of just threw money at the problem.
"... There was not a defined culture and North Star where we were going [as an organization]," Ishbia concluded. "And therefore, bringing in super-talented players like Kevin Durant doesn't necessarily lead to championships."Does Ishbia have a point?Of course he does. In fact, he didn't even really need the "necessarily" qualification. Unless we're talking about the Warriors (who had Stephen Curry, and, by extension, the sort of foundational championship culture to which Ishbia is referring, and were therefore an exception to this rule), bringing in Durant has definitively not led to championships -- or frankly even honest championship contention. Not for the Nets. Not for the Suns. And so far, not for the Rockets. That's not the dig on Durant that it sounds like. Throughout NBA history, there are very few examples of a team without an incumbent championship superstar winning a ring by way of a hired hand. The 2016 Cavaliers and 2020 Lakers did it with LeBron James, who's the ultimate exception to this rule. He wins everywhere he goes. It's one of the brightest feathers in his GOAT-case cap. 
Other than that, you've got Kawhi Leonard in Toronto, Jalen Brunson in New York, and Kevin Garnett and Ray Allen with the 2008 Celtics as the only examples this century. It just doesn't often happen that a mercenary superstar parachutes into an organization and delivers a title, and certainly not right away. Brunson needed four years and a slew of significant roster moves around him to make it happen with the Knicks. Because Ishbia is right. You generally need an established culture with the right support system, from the role players to the coaches and the front office, in place first. Doing it the other way around is like trying to build a skyscraper on a crap foundation, and we've seen such structures fail over and over. James Harden with, well, every team he's ever gone to after Houston, including Durant's Nets, is the perfect example. All of which is to say, when Ishbia says "bringing in super-talented players like Kevin Durant doesn't necessarily lead to championships," he's just telling the truth. It's pretty convenient, now that we all know how it turned out, that he's saying he never wanted to go the Durant route in the first place, but nonetheless, he's admitting that he messed up in trying to microwave the Suns like an overnight fantasy team. 
You can't do that these days. Especially with the way the aprons are restricting expensive roster building moving forward. There's a reason we don't see teams depleting their rosters -- as the Suns did in offloading the likes of Mikal Bridges, Cam Johnson, Chris Paul, Jae Crowder and Deandre Ayton from their 2021 Finals team -- just to service their superstar fetishes anymore. All Ishbia is saying is he has learned from his own mistakes how important roster depth, coaching and culture are to a championship pursuit, and that even an all-time talent like Durant isn't enough to overcome the absence of those organizational elements. Does Durant have a point, too?In this case, not really. He's right that he "stayed on top of his game at 36" and was individually spectacular in his two and a half seasons with the Suns, as he has been for his entire career, but Ishbia never attacked his personal performance. In fact, he never really personally attacked Durant at all, although you can understand the offense a Hall of Famer would take to being painted as a player with less "Suns DNA," which is code for winning DNA, than Brooks and Gillespie. 
But the bottom line is the Suns, with guys like Brooks and Gillespie playing their ass off every single night, were a better team last year without Durant than they were with him the year prior when they won 36 games and missed the playoffs. Frankly, it's almost baffling that Durant could say with a straight face that he brought the culture back to Ishbia and the Suns. In the two and a half seasons before Durant arrived, the Suns were a model franchise that had made the Finals, finished as the West's No. 1 and No. 2 seeds in consecutive seasons, and won nearly 70% of their regular-season games. In the two and a half years with Durant, they lost nearly half their regular-season games, and in the two full seasons they had him, they got swept in the first round and missed the playoffs entirely. That's not to say any of that was Durant's fault, at least in the sense that he was always individually excellent on the court. Reasonable minds can disagree as to the additive power of Durant's particular basketball brand (it's a question of how much he raises the level of those around him), but never his own production. It's just impossible to compete for championships without all your organizational I's dotted and T's crossed. 
That's the lesson Ishbia is saying he has learned. That you can't win by "throwing money" at your problems. It probably applies more to the Bradley Beal disaster than the trade for Durant, but the general point is the same. You have to fix these problems from the inside out, and the simple truth is that Durant has been parachuting in from the outside trying to save dying teams since he left Golden State. Almost nobody succeeds in that mission. Not even one of the 10-15 greatest players to ever live, as many, including myself, believe Durant to be.

title: College football winners, losers in Week 7: BYU is the toast of historic weekend, Texas has a Sark problem - CBS Sports

body:
BYU makes its case as a national title contender, Auburn stuns Georgia in Athens and Sarkisian searches for answers after another ugly Longhorns loss
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 18, 2026
                            
                    at
    9:36 am ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Any given Saturday can be an earth-shattering moment in college football history. Week 7 was one for the ages. Five of the top seven teams in the AP top 25 rankings went down, completely shaking up the national championship pictureLeading the way, No. 8 BYU stunned No. 2 Notre Dame in heavyweight battle. No. 4 Ohio State was also able to outlast No. 5 Indiana. Losses by No. 1 Georgia, No. 6 Alabama and No. 7 Texas are a little less forgivable. After the carnage, UCLA is the only remaining undefeated in the Big Ten or SEC. The battle for number one in the AP top 25 should be fierce as undefeated Miami and BYU contend with a wave of one loss teams. With that in mind, here are the biggest winners and losers of Week 7. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: BYU Since 2024, BYU has been the third-winningest program in college football. Still, they haven't been treated as a legitimate national-caliber program. After a stirring 28-24 upset over No. 2 Notre Dame, the Cougars officially clinched their spot among the national elite. 
BYU dominated in nearly every area of the game, including holding opposing quarterback CJ Carr to 27-of-49 passing. Sophomore quarterback Bear Bachmeier led a game-winning drive with only minutes remaining to seal the deal.With the win, BYU is assured a spot in the College Football Playoff assuming it takes care of business and could jump into the AP's top-three rankings for the first time since their national championship season in 1984. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Loser: Texas coach Steve SarkisianSarkisian has done nearly everything in his power to avoid taking responsibility over the last two seasons. After yet another stunning loss to Florida, the shine is fully coming off.
Texas' offensive game plan looked disastrous against the Florida defense ranked among the worst in the SEC. Longhorns quarterback Arch Manning has not developed in any meaningful way and continues to make mistakes at the worst possible time. After the loss to Oklahoma, Sarkisian said that there's "not a chance" that he gives up play-calling. After the Florida loss, he admitted everything was up for evaluation. With a second loss on the record, there may not be another choice. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: Ole Miss The Rebels were backsliding a little bit after their quality wins over LSU and Louisville quickly fell out a favor. But after a total decimation of Missouri, 31-3, Ole Miss is suddenly right back in the SEC race.
Specifically, it was the defense that took center stage after a few weeks of poor performance. The Rebels pounced, holding a stacked Missouri running game to 1.5 yards per carry. Star Mizzou running back Jamal Roberts didn't have a single rush of more than six yards. Ole Miss's offense is going to be fine. If the defense is finally reaching championship caliber again, that changes things. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Loser: BaylorBaylor coach Dave Aranda seemed to get firmly off the hot seat after a strong start to the season. But after a 17-6 loss to a struggling TCU squad, the Bears are suddenly dead in the water.
Technically, Baylor only has one loss in Big 12 play, but the loss of momentum after losing to a hated rival will be harder to overcome. The Bears got the absolute worst of the DJ Lagway experience as he completed fewer than 50% of his passes and Baylor's offense mustered only six total points.It's unclear how Baylor will handle Aranda's job status in the weeks ahead but with BYU, Texas Tech and Houston still on the schedule, plenty more losses are ahead. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: Auburn The Tigers have needed something good to happen for so long. Auburn hadn't beaten George in Athens in 21 years, but Alex Golesh helped get them over the finish line behind a strong defensive effort. 
Auburn was able to bait Bulldogs QB Gunner Stockton into a pair of interceptions for great field position, and also got 100 yards on the ground from its own QB, Byrum Brown. Georgia was favored by 20.5 pounds against the Tigers. Instead, Auburn won 27-24. Its roster is starting to come together. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Loser: QB Keelon Russell, AlabamaAfter five straight games of at least 45 points to open the year, quarterback Keelon Russell is struggling. The sophomore threw for just 147 yards and two interceptions in a 26-10 loss to Tennessee. Finishing with a less efficient day than counterpart George McIntyre was a rough look. The Crimson Tide's blazing start is slipping as the offense finished with only 201 total yards. Tennessee's defense is strong, but Russell's slip in Knoxville remains puzzling. Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer must get things figured out or the Tide's season could quickly end. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: North CarolinaDon't look now, but the Tar Heels are suddenly looking pretty impressive. The Tar Heels upset reigning ACC champion and chief rival Duke on Saturday, 24-20, to continue a strong flurry of recent performances -- last week, Bill Belichick got his first ranked win on the road vs. Pitt. The Blue Devils both outgained UNC and won the turnover margin, but North Carolina managed to overcome early miscues to pick up wins. Now, the Tar Heels are 4-2. Belichick deserves plenty of credit. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: RutgersThe battle between Rutgers and Maryland was one of the tightest ever for worst in the Power Four, but the Scarlet Knights emerged as the champion in a back-and-forth game against the Terrapins, 37-30. 
Really, Rutgers has the benefit of wide receiver KJ Duff, maybe the best wide receiver outside of Jeremiah Smith. The senior caught nine passes for 113 yards and two touchdowns. While Duff will certainly soon be catching passes from NFL passers, it's nice to see him stack Rutgers records. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: ArkansasIt only took three years, but Arkansas finally has its first SEC win in ages. The Razorbacks outlasted Vanderbilt, 31-21, behind 300 total yards from quarterback KJ Jackson. Arkansas had not won a single SEC game since their bowl season in 2024, but already-embattled first-year coach Ryan Silverfield finally has something to sell.

body:
The advantage of betting on awards is that they are comparatively predictable. No, I cannot tell you with perfect accuracy who the 2027 NBA MVP will be... but I can tell you how the prior winners have been selected. Awards voters are humans. Humans are predictable, even if performance is not. While there will be injuries and unexpected candidates and circumstantial changes we can't yet foresee, we can at least use the history of these awards to land on the type of players who tend to win them, and then work backward from there.So we're going to reverse engineer some best bets for NBA awards season now that opening night is nearly upon us. These are not, strictly, NBA awards picks. If you could pick one player to win Defensive Player of the Year, for example, you should pick Victor Wembanyama. But if you're trying to find the best return on investment in that category, paying minus money on the hope that Wembanyama plays 65 games seems like a high-risk, low-reward proposition. The goal here is to find the players that best fit the prior history of these awards in a way that maximizes profit. With all of that in mind, let's begin.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    MVP: Luka Dončić, Lakers (+600)
The MVP formula points very clearly toward a single candidate this year. Every MVP since LeBron James in 2012 has checked two boxes: they have been between the ages of 24 and 28, and they were either a First- or Second-Team All-NBA selection in the prior season. That's essentially the criteria: a top-10 player in the previous season peaks at some point in his prime and gets a trophy. Victor Wembanyama is too young (and has the shortest odds... and carries 65-game concerns). Nikola Jokić is too old. 
Only three players check both boxes. The first is two-time defending champion Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who's facing the notable challenge of seeking his third consecutive trophy. Nobody has won three straight MVPs since Larry Bird, and that became a major topic when Jokić tried and failed to three-peat in 2023. It's not fair, but Gilgeous-Alexander is going to get held to a ridiculous standard. Michael Jordan and LeBron James couldn't go three-for-three, and there will be voters who hold that against Gilgeous-Alexander.The second is Cade Cunningham. He has by far the longest odds of the three, but he has the most working against him as well. It's very hard to repeat as a 60-game winner. The Thunder and Celtics are the only teams to do it this century, and in addition to having superior rosters, they didn't have to deal with a tanking-free NBA. The Pistons, thanks to lottery reform, will. Win totals are going to be deflated, especially in a loaded Eastern Conference. It wouldn't take much actual decline for the Pistons to fall from 60 to 50 wins, and there's room for notable decline here. Will Jalen Duren repeat last year's performance after an offseason-long contract standoff? Can they sustain the losses of key role players like Tobias Harris and Isaiah Stewart? And of course, Cunningham isn't in the sort of offense-first environment that tends to lead to MVP stats. This is a defensive-minded team that starts two non-shooters.That leaves us with Dončić, the seemingly perpetual offseason favorite. The Lakers have finally built him the sort of team he wants: an imposing rim protector at center (Walker Kessler), a second, star-level creator (Austin Reaves) and plenty of shooting everywhere else. The Lakers have plenty of ball-handling redundancy to keep the offense afloat when he rests. Dončić averaged nearly 34 points, eight rebounds and eight assists after Jan. 1, so the numbers should be MVP-level. LeBron is gone. The team is finally his.
We all know the Wembanyama era is coming. If it's at all close, there will be voter sympathy behind the idea of sneaking one last winner in before we assume the trophy gets its next dynastic winner. There are real 65-game fears (he needed an appeal to sneak past that threshold last season), and backup center is a concern here that could cost the Lakers games in the standings. But Dončić checks the historical boxes, will likely have the biggest raw numbers, plays for a glamour franchise and is about as due for an MVP award as any player has ever been. He might be the best player who's never won one. Now is his best chance.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Defensive Player of the Year: Bam Adebayo, Heat (+4000)
Alright, let's have the Wembanyama conversation. If he plays 65 games, he wins. Any objections? No? Cool. You're paying -330 odds for the privilege of hoping he stays healthy, which implies odds of just under 77% that he wins. So what we're really asking here is if there's a 77% chance that Victor Wembanyama plays 65 games. I would lean no for a few reasons:A total of 166 players participated in 65 or more games last season. A total of 579 players played in at least one game, so a bit more than a quarter of all NBA players played 65 games last season. Now, that's not a fair sample here since it includes two-ways, 10-days and other cup of coffee types rather than real NBA players. Let's reduce our sample. Exactly 209 players started at least 20 games a season ago... and only 120, or 57.4%, reached 65 games. In other words, even for a standard player, the odds of reaching 65 games are probably below 77%.From a health standpoint, Wembanyama probably isn't a standard player. He's the tallest player in the league, and historically speaking, players that big tend to be injury-prone. Wembanyama has been more durable than most thus far. That doesn't eliminate the risk entirely.Wembanyama's rookie extension includes no Rose Rule bonuses. He has no financial incentive to push to play 65 games for an individual award. If it's close, especially after they lost the Finals a year ago, the Spurs will prioritize health for the postseason.So if your life depended on it and you just needed to pick someone? Yes. Take Wembanyama. His odds just don't reflect his actual chances.
So, who are we looking for in the "non-Wembanyama" weight class? For starters, the responsible choice is always a center. Every decade, we tend to get one non-rim-protector winner (even if that player wins more than once). It was Gary Payton in the 1990s, Ron Artest in the 2000s, Kawhi Leonard in the 2010s, and Marcus Smart in the 2020s. We've already acknowledged perimeter play this decade, and the Smart award has aged badly enough to scare off some voters. We're also looking for a top-five defense. Every winner since 2008 has played for one except Evan Mobley in 2025... who only won because Wembanyama had a blood clot, and even he was on an anomalous 64-win team.So who are the rim protectors on likely top-five defenses? I projected the Spurs, Thunder, Pistons, Raptors and Heat as the top-five defenses for this season. We've already covered San Antonio's candidate. Oklahoma City's Chet Holmgren has the next lowest odds at +1200, but he has the disadvantage of playing on a historically loaded defense. Assigning credit to a single Thunder defender feels reductive, and fair or not, playoff performance is absolutely held against players in this race. It's not a coincidence that Rudy Gobert lost this award in 2022, right after he was unfairly blamed for the hottest shooting night of Terance Mann's life. Holmgren is still washing the stink of the Western Conference Finals off of himself.Detroit's candidate is a non-center, Ausar Thompson. In truth, I'd call him the NBA's second-best defender. That doesn't mean voting will reflect that, especially since the absence of Isaiah Stewart hurts the defense on balance. Besides, Thompson's fouling and offensive vulnerabilities tend to prevent him from playing the sort of minutes someone needs to win this award. Scottie Barnes does play enough minutes, but, in part because of his offensive responsibilities, he isn't quite as impactful defensively as Thompson is. The stars need to align perfectly for a non-center, and they don't in Barnes' case.
That leaves Miami's center, Bam Adebayo, who has spent years complaining about how he doesn't have one of these awards yet. Well, this is his best chance. Miami has one of the best defensive lineups in the NBA. Giannis Antetokounmpo has won this award, but he has declined just enough not to compete with Adebayo for this year's. Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins are legitimate plus starters, and Erik Spoelstra might be the NBA's most creative defensive coach. Adebayo doesn't post gaudy block or steal numbers, and the all-in-ones usually nudge him below the top handful of defensive bigs, but the eye test is obviously favorable and, as with Dončić, there will be a sense that he's due if he comes close. At 40-to-1, this is one of the better value plays on the board.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Rookie of the Year: Caleb Wilson, Bulls (+350)
Rookie of the Year is historically a counting stats award. Playing for a winning team almost never factors in, as the race between Cooper Flagg and Kon Knueppel last year, or Victor Wembanyama vs. Chet Holmgren three seasons ago, demonstrates. In the past two decades, the only Rookie of the Year winners to average fewer than 15 points per game have been Malcolm Brogdon, who only won because Joel Embiid got hurt, and Stephon Castle, who won in a historically weak class. Therefore, we're looking for opportunity first and foremost.That immediately rules out AJ Dybantsa of the Wizards and Darryn Peterson of the Jazz. The former is on a team with two veteran stars and several younger players still trying to make their mark in the league. The latter plays with another high-usage guard who just signed a long-term extension and two veteran star forwards. They're going to be great, but they're going to have fewer opportunities.
That leaves us three viable candidates. Darius Acuff Jr. has the longest odds outside of the top four, and he's probably going to lead all rookies in shot attempts simply because he plays for the Kings. Of course, that's a bit of a double-edged sword in this respect. He'll likely be the least efficient of the candidates for the same reason, and while that doesn't matter in some races, this one will likely be too competitive for a player to get away with putting up empty numbers.Cameron Boozer is the most pro-ready rookie in this class. He swept the National Player of the Year awards in college a season ago, and most of the analytical models pegged him as clearly the best prospect in this class. Memphis probably has the most available shots among these teams. The concern here is slight, but statistically notable. The Grizzlies simply don't play their players as many minutes as most other teams do. Tuomas Iisalo believes in limiting players to four- or five-minute bursts. If you ignore the tanking players they used at the end of the year, Jaren Jackson Jr. led the Grizzlies with only 30.7 minutes per game last year. If Boozer plays four or five fewer minutes per night than the other candidates, that could create a counting stats disadvantage.Caleb Wilson is handling the ball quite a bit in the preseason. The Bulls are seemingly putting him through the suddenly common "what if we point guard-ified our top forward prospect" arc that Flagg endured a year ago and Giannis Antetokounmpo popularized a decade ago. That approach tends to come with growing pains, but as Flagg can attest, it is not disqualifying in the Rookie of the Year race. If anything, the volume is helpful. Wilson likely won't have the ball as much as Flagg did a season ago, but he's on a roster that makes more sense and should be more conducive to his success. You're getting slightly better odds on Wilson than you are on Boozer. It's a justifiable matter of preference between the two. Boozer is the safer pick. Wilson's upside and longer odds push him over the top for me.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Coach of the Year: Joe Mazzulla, Celtics (+2500)Here's where we start to defy history in one notable way: nobody has ever repeated as Coach of the Year. Not Gregg Popovich. Not Phil Jackson. Not Pat Riley. Not Red Auerbach. That's why Mazzulla's odds are this long, and those odds are why he's such an easy pick. He's the NBA's best regular-season coach. I'm happy to take the 25-to-1 swing on someone this good defying history.Mazzulla's offense has ranked either No. 1 or No. 2 in all four of his seasons at the helm for the Celtics. He maintained that excellence a season ago largely without his best player, Jayson Tatum, and with half of his 2024 championship rotation gone. His approach produces regular-season wins en masse. The Celtics shoot more 3s than almost everyone. They get more offensive rebounds than almost everyone. They protect the rim better than almost everyone. They never turn the ball over.The Jaylen Brown trade will be enormously helpful to Mazzulla's case. It is simultaneously the narrative trigger that a coach would need to defy the "nobody has repeated" history and a move made to further mold the team in Mazzulla's image. Paul George fits much more cleanly into the whole "shoot a million 3s and never turn the ball over" scheme than Brown does. Mitchell Robinson only amplifies Boston's success protecting the basket on one end and owning the glass on the other. No roster more cleanly matches its coach's stylistic preferences than this one.
Every Coach of the Year winner since Doc Rivers in 2000 has been a top-four seed. Most of them are top-two seeds, and the formula is quite often "the most surprising of the four best regular-season teams." Well, nobody is going to be surprised when the Spurs and Thunder capture the top two Western Conference seeds. The shock of the Brown trade has worn off. Plenty of people expect the Celtics to have a very successful regular season. But it generated more than enough doubt to vault Mazzulla into a historic repeat if he pulls this off.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Sixth Man of the Year: Daniss Jenkins, Pistons (+5000)
The favorites here are all obvious starting candidates. Payton Pritchard and Dylan Harper might be opening night starters, and even if they're not, they could force the issue relatively early. Ajay Mitchell is an injury away, but the Thunder tend to be cautious when their players get hurt. They rest key players frequently, and it's not hard to imagine a world in which Mitchell starts half of the season purely through filling in for teammates. And as is the case for Holmgren with Defensive Player of the Year, it's hard to assign too much credit to a single Thunder reserve for their bench dominance. Mitchell will score the points, but does that mean he's a better player than Alex Caruso? Jared McCain is a starting-level player. Jaylin Williams might be as well. That's a hard roster to stand out on.Our last six winners have come from top-three seeds, so we want someone on a winning roster. We also want scoring, as 10 of the 17 winners between 2006 and 2022 were that season's leading bench scorer. We haven't had a season's leading bench scorer win since, but pure point total is always a factor in this race. You win by coming off the bench for a winner and scoring a lot of points.
The last four winners have hovered around the 13-15-point per game mark. Jenkins wasn't there most of last season, but he averaged 19 points per game in relief of the injured Cade Cunningham for a key stretch late last year. He's not going to start often this year, but think about the Pistons roster. He's really the only proven, secondary ball-handler now that Tobias Harris and Caris LeVert are gone. Unless Ebuka Okorie is ready faster than we're anticipating, the sheer volume of dribbling opportunities available to Jenkins this season is going to be absolutely enormous for a bench player. At 50-to-1, that sort of volume on a team this good is too tempting to pass up.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Most Improved Player: Coby White, Hornets (+4500)
Most Improved Player can typically be distilled into "the first-time All-Star" award. The last two winners bucked that trend, as the Hawks won with Dyson Daniels and Nickeil Alexander-Walker. Before that? Our previous five winners were first-time All-Stars. The catch with that definition this season is that none of the obvious first-time All-Star candidates make sense through the award's other typical standards.Austin Reaves has a great chance at making his first All-Star Team this season. He's already received votes for this award in two separate seasons. You can't be a candidate for this award every year. Cooper Flagg is another consensus pick as a possible first-time All-Star, but he's in his second season. No second-year player has won this award since Monta Ellis in 2007, but Ellis was a second-round pick. Flagg is literally the reigning Rookie of the Year. It's possible and perhaps probable that a player truly does come out of nowhere to make an All-Star Team. That player becomes the favorite. For now, we're working off of opportunity and circumstance.
Coby White has had All-Star-esque stretches. He averaged almost 28 points per game in March 2025, right after the Bulls traded Zach LaVine and handed him and Josh Giddey the keys to the offense. He won't be that good over the full season, but it goes to show that White, when entrusted to run an offense, can post absolutely bonkers numbers. He's playing on a team with shooting everywhere. The Hornets have a real chance to break the 3-point attempt record. With Ball gone, creation is at a premium in Charlotte. White is going to be the player responsible for creating most of those 3-point attempts. He'll have a hard time actually making the All-Star team simply because Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel are ahead of him in the team's overall pecking order and this team isn't going to be good enough for multiple All-Stars, but if the Hornets exceed expectations and White posts huge numbers in the process, a 45-to-1 ticket is going to feel very valuable.

body:
A look at how national championship contenders fared in Week 7 action
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 18, 2026
                            
                    at
    9:41 am ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        On a day of carnage and drama for top-10 teams, No. 9 Ole Miss quietly but commandingly made itself an exception by dominating No. 13 Missouri for a 31-3 victory. The Rebels trailed 3-0 but never again as they owned both lines of scrimmage, improving to 5-1 (3-1 SEC).The "how" behind the win stood out for the right reasons. In particular, star running back Kewan Lacy surpassed 100 yards rushing for the first time in 2026. After an injury-plagued beginning to his season, Lacy torched the Tigers for 122 yards rushing on 16 carries as the Rebels rode a balanced attack to a commanding win.Star quarterback Trinidad Chambliss brought his usual fireworks with four total touchdowns. But if Ole Miss is going to make a second straight College Football Playoff appearance, it will need more of the offensive diversity that it flashed against Mizzou. With +1600 title odds coming out of Week 7, the Rebels remain firmly in the mix as they gear up for a trip to face a reeling Texas team.We are handing out grades evaluating every team that started or ended the day with national championship odds of +3000 or better. 
2026 national championship odds listed below courtesy of FanDuel Sportsbook. Teams listed in order of their AP Top 25 ranking.   
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 1 GeorgiaGrade: F  Result: 27-24 loss vs. Auburn  Title odds: +490One easy way to lose a game when favored by 20.5 points is to give your opponent a 3-0 edge in turnover margin. That's what Georgia did, as senior quarterback Gunner Stockton coughed it up three times. The last giveaway led directly to Auburn's game-winning field goal as time expired. UGA's defense finally figured things out in the second half to give the Bulldogs a chance. But those pesky turnovers made the difference. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 2 Notre DameGrade: C-  Result: 28-24 loss at BYU  Title odds: +460Notre Dame's vaunted defense allowed BYU to convert on 8 of 12 third downs and surrendered a late go-ahead touchdown drive. The Fighting Irish's offense had scoring opportunities at the end of both halves but came up empty. It was an evening of missed opportunities for Marcus Freeman's club, which settled for field goals after two horrendous special teams blunders by the Cougars in the third quarter. The aura of invincibility which surrounded this team entering Week 7 was shattered by a team with less talent. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 3 MiamiGrade: C  Result: 43-35 (OT) win vs. Florida State  Title odds: +600Miami racked up 583 yards, won the turnover battle and dominated time of possession but still needed overtime (and a controversial overtime ending) to outlast its in-state rival. The 'Canes gave up way too many explosive plays, and the offense's inability to finish drives in the third quarter made this game more dramatic than it should have been.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 4 Ohio StateGrade: B-  Result: 19-15 win at Indiana  Title odds: +500This was a pass/fail assignment for Ohio State, which is now in possession of a gold-plated win that will define its resume. The best thing the Buckeyes did was take away Indiana's rushing game, which is no small feat. IU's star tandem of Turbo Richard and Lee Beebe Jr. combined for just 70 yards on 25 carries. Otherwise, it was an ugly slog. But earning a 'B-' in a road win over a top-5 team is like earning a B- in advanced trigonometry. The main goal is to pass, and Ohio State passed. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 5 IndianaGrade: C  Result: 19-15 loss vs. Ohio State  Title odds: +900Indiana's star backs combined for just 70 yards and did not produce a run of more than seven yards as the Hoosiers became one-dimensional. With quarterback Josh Hoover battling early inaccuracy and then a shoulder injury, life looked too hard for the IU offense. The defense negated Jeremiah Smith's impact all game until he corralled a 38-yard touchdown pass with 12:46 remaining to give Ohio State a two-possession lead. That was a backbreaker in a game ultimately decided by inches.  

                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 6 AlabamaGrade: D  Result: 26-10 loss at Tennessee  Title odds: +1100Alabama was physically dominated on both sides of the ball. The offensive line couldn't open up running lanes or protect Keelon Russell, who looked rattled early. The defense was rarely disruptive in the backfield -- amassing just two tackles for loss -- and couldn't get off the field in the fourth quarter. A week after a physically grueling loss to Georgia, the Crimson Tide looked hungover and unprepared for Tennessee's brand of smashmouth football. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 7 TexasGrade: F  Result: 27-24 loss vs. Florida  Title odds: +1400Playing at home against a struggling Florida team using its backup quarterback, Texas surrendered 24 unanswered points while relinquishing a 17-3 lead. The vaunted Texas defense couldn't rattle inexperienced Gators QB Tramell Jones, and the Longhorns looked putrid offensively. Senior quarterback Arch Manning continues to struggle, and head coach Steve Sarkisian has no answers. This was a stunning and inexcusable outcome for the nation's former No. 1 team, which has now dropped two straight against unranked opposition. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 9 Ole MissGrade: AResult: 31-3 win vs. MissouriTitle odds: +1600Kewan Lacy and Makhi Frazier each surpassed 100 yards rushing as Ole Miss dominated the line of scrimmage by averaging 6.8 yards per rush against a Missouri defense that had been good against the run. Conversely, the Rebels bottled up Jamal Roberts, who entered as the SEC's leading rusher. The end result was a drama-free victory for Ole Miss, which got four total touchdowns from star quarterback Trinidad Chambliss.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 22 LSUGrade: AResult: 31-0 win vs. Mississippi StateTitle odds: +2200Injuries to Mississippi State's offensive stars created a layup that LSU could ill-afford to miss. The Tigers handled the assignment by jumping out to a quick 14-0 lead and never looking back. The Bulldogs repeatedly found their way into LSU territory, but the Tigers played elite fourth-down defense. Offensively, quarterback Sam Leavitt finished interception-free for the first time in his seven games as the starter.
